source_refs.note: Topic 8.5, printed pages 184-187: uptake by roots, the three pathways, the structure of xylem and the TACT mechanism. The phloem cells of Figure 8.10 share the xylem-phloem original with topic 8.6.

blocks.text: Roots provide a large surface area for absorption through their extensive branching. Root hairs, extensions of the epidermal cells of the root, carry out most of the uptake of water and minerals. From the soil, water and minerals enter the root epidermal cells by active and passive transport, move through the cortex and reach the xylem at the centre of the root. Inside the root they travel by three different pathways.

items: The apoplast pathway is a continuous route through the system of adjacent cell walls of the root. It becomes discontinuous at the endodermis because of the Casparian strips there.

In the symplast pathway, water and minerals move through the interconnected protoplasts of the root cells, linked by plasmodesmata, cytoplasmic strands that pass through pores in adjacent cell walls. The symplast pathway is less important except for minerals in the region of the endodermis.

In the vacuolar pathway, water and minerals cross cell membranes, cytoplasm, tonoplasts (vacuole membranes) and vacuoles, moving from vacuole to vacuole and bypassing the symplast and apoplast. Movement by this pathway is negligible.

blocks.alt: A root hair cell on the left, four cortex cells with vacuoles, an endodermis cell with brown Casparian strips on its sides, and the xylem on the right. An orange line along the cell walls stops at the Casparian strip with a block symbol; a purple line runs through the cytoplasm of every cell into the xylem; a dashed blue line passes through the vacuoles.
blocks.caption: The apoplast, symplast and vacuolar pathways across the root (original diagram after Figure 8.7).
blocks.long_description: Water enters at the root hair and crosses the cortex to the xylem by three routes. The apoplast route runs along the cell walls and is stopped at the endodermis by the waterproof Casparian strip. The symplast route passes from cytoplasm to cytoplasm through plasmodesmata and so crosses the endodermis. The vacuolar route goes from vacuole to vacuole across membranes and tonoplasts and carries a negligible amount.

blocks.text: Xylem is the vascular tissue that carries water and dissolved minerals from the roots to the stem and leaves; it is also a key structural tissue that gives mechanical support. It comprises tracheids, vessels, xylem fibres and xylem parenchyma. Tracheids are elongated, thin cells with thick lignified walls; their ends are tapered and they are linked by bordered pits that allow water to move laterally between cells. Vessels are shorter and broader, arranged end to end to form continuous channels, with perforation plates at their ends for efficient water movement. Xylem fibres are elongated cells with thickened lignified walls, dead at maturity, which add to the structural strength of the xylem. Xylem parenchyma cells are living, thin-walled cells that retain water and nutrients, take part in lateral translocation and help in the healing and regeneration of the xylem.

blocks.alt: Left, four xylem cells: a long tapered tracheid with bordered pits, a wide vessel of stacked elements with perforation plates, a dark lignified fibre and small living parenchyma cells. Right, four phloem cells: a sieve tube of stacked elements with dotted sieve plates, companion cells beside it linked by short lines, a phloem fibre and parenchyma.
blocks.caption: The cells of xylem and of phloem (original diagram after Figures 8.8 and 8.10).
blocks.long_description: Xylem: tracheids are long, thin, lignified cells with tapered ends and bordered pits for sideways flow; vessels are shorter, broader elements joined end to end through perforation plates; fibres have thick lignified walls and are dead, adding strength; parenchyma cells are living, store water and nutrients and move them sideways. Phloem: sieve tube elements join end to end through sieve plates into a sieve tube; each has companion cells linked by plasmodesmata that supply ATP and proteins; phloem fibres support, and phloem parenchyma stores sugars, resins, latex and mucilage.

blocks.text: The movement of water through the xylem

Water moves from the roots to the leaves mainly through the xylem. The TACT mechanism (Transpiration, Adhesion, Cohesion, Tension) is the widely accepted model of how water moves against gravity through the xylem to every part of the plant; it depends on the physical and chemical properties of water and on the plant's interaction with its environment.

items: Transpiration is the evaporation of water from the surface of the leaves, specifically through the stomata. As water vapour leaves the leaf, a negative pressure develops in the leaf tissue; this pulling force draws water upward from the roots through the stem towards the leaves, so transpiration is the primary driving force of water transport in the xylem.

Adhesion is the attraction between water molecules and the walls of the xylem vessels. Water molecules stick to the walls as they move upward, preventing any break in the water column and keeping it continuous, especially in tall plants where gravity pulls strongly on the column.

Cohesion is the attractive force between water molecules themselves, caused by hydrogen bonding. The water molecules in the xylem stick together in an unbroken column from roots to leaves, so the pull started by transpiration at the leaf extends down the whole column.

Tension is the negative pressure created by the pull of transpiration at the leaf. As water evaporates from the leaf surface, a low-pressure area extends through the xylem, and this tension pulls the cohesive water column upwards; it is vital for the continuous ascent of water.

blocks.alt: A xylem vessel drawn as a tall tube from roots at the bottom to a leaf at the top. Blue water molecules form a dotted chain up the tube, with orange ticks where they touch the walls; a grey arrow beside it points up; blue arrows show water entering the roots and water vapour leaving the leaf. The four parts of TACT are labelled on the right.
blocks.caption: The TACT mechanism of water flow from root to leaf (original diagram after Figure 8.9).
blocks.long_description: Transpiration through the stomata creates a negative pressure in the leaf. Adhesion holds the water to the xylem walls so the column does not break; cohesion by hydrogen bonds joins the water molecules into one unbroken column; and the tension transmitted down that column pulls water up from the roots against gravity, where it entered the root hairs by osmosis.

blocks.caption: The four parts of TACT
rows: Evaporation of water through the stomata
Creates the negative pressure that drives the whole flow
Attraction of water to the xylem walls
Keeps the column continuous against gravity
Makes one unbroken column so the pull reaches the roots
Negative pressure extending down the xylem

blocks.prompt: A tree's leaves are sprayed with a substance that seals the stomata. Using TACT, explain what happens to the flow of water in its xylem.
blocks.explanation: Sealed stomata stop transpiration, so no water vapour leaves and no negative pressure forms in the leaf. Without that tension there is nothing to pull the cohesive water column up; adhesion and cohesion keep the column intact but stationary, so the upward flow of water through the xylem largely stops.

items: Root hairs take up water and minerals; across the root they travel by the apoplast (cell walls, blocked at the endodermis by the Casparian strip), the symplast (cytoplasm through plasmodesmata) or the negligible vacuolar pathway.

Xylem: tracheids (tapered, bordered pits), vessels (end to end with perforation plates), fibres (lignified, dead, support) and parenchyma (living, storage, lateral movement, repair). Also a structural tissue.
TACT: transpiration creates tension; adhesion to the walls and cohesion between molecules keep an unbroken column that the tension pulls up from root to leaf.
